strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: removing the need for manually annotated masks/bounding boxes in 6D pose estimation and tracking pipelines, which is a genuine deployment bottleneck for methods like FoundationPose.

The overall system design combining a segmentation module (SOM) guided by rendered multi-view references + language semantics with a tracking module (TOM) that explicitly monitors and recovers from tracking failure is a sensible and useful integration, addressing a real gap (lack of failure-detection/re-registration in prior trackers).

Fairly comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 BOP core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V) with numerous supervised/unsupervised baselines (Table 2), plus dedicated pose-estimation comparisons (Table 1) and tracking-recovery experiments (Tables 3-4).
Reasonable ablations in the appendix (language injection, HSFA depth, DINOv2 fine-tuning) that partially justify design choices and show speed/accuracy trade-offs.
Contribution of a new tracking-failure classification dataset (with clearly described construction protocol) that could be useful to the community for benchmarking tracking robustness.
Real-time inference numbers are reported (0.183s for SOM, ~13ms overhead for TOM), which supports the practical significance claim if verified.
weaknesses: Central terminology/soundness inconsistency: the paper repeatedly claims STORM is "annotation-free"/"self-supervised" and requires "no manual annotation," yet Section 3's loss formulation (Eq. 2-3) explicitly uses ground-truth pixel labels t for Tversky/Focal loss, and Appendix D confirms per-pixel mask-based training. This is standard supervised segmentation training on rendered/labeled data, not self-supervision; the categorization in Table 2 as "self-supervised" (contrasted favorably against "supervised" baselines) appears to mischaracterize the method and inflates the apparent novelty/advantage over supervised competitors.

Potential train/test overlap: Appendix C states SOM is trained on "a combined subset of the LMO, LM, YCBV, HB, TLESS, TUDL, TYOL, RU-APC" datasets, and the main segmentation evaluation (Q2, Table 2) is performed on "LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-Light, HomebrewedDB, YCB-Video" — the same benchmark families. The paper does not clearly explain how object identity/instance separation between train and test splits was ensured, raising concerns about data leakage that could explain the surprising result of a zero-shot method outperforming per-object fine-tuned supervised baselines (ZebraPose) on 4/5 datasets.

No code or dataset link is actually provided ("Code:" field is empty), and the promised tracking dataset release is not accompanied by any concrete access information, undermining reproducibility despite claims of open-sourcing.

Ablation studies (Appendix E) use different training budgets (20 epochs) than the main results (80,000 steps on 8×A100), making it unclear whether conclusions (e.g., HSFA3 vs HSFA7, language injection benefit) transfer to the actual deployed configuration.

Limited comparison scope for tracking: TOM/re-registration is only compared against vanilla FoundationPose tracking (Table 3) and a cosine-similarity baseline (Table 4); no comparison to other modern re-detection or recovery strategies (e.g., Siam R-CNN-style re-detection, other pose trackers with failure recovery) is provided, limiting the strength of the tracking-robustness claims.

Statistical rigor is weak: most tables report single-run point estimates without variance/confidence intervals (only Table 3 includes ± on timing, not accuracy), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (e.g., STORM 68.5 vs ZebraPose 67.5 mAP) are meaningful or within noise.

The system pipeline is complex (LLM + CLIP + DINOv2 + HSFA + SAM2 + FoundationPose + separate tracking-loss classifier), and while individual components are ablated, there is no end-to-end latency/accuracy breakdown showing how errors compound across stages, nor a discussion of failure modes when the VLM-generated semantic description is inaccurate.

Claims of generalization to "novel objects" are not tested on any dataset/object categories entirely disjoint from BOP-style industrial/household objects used in training and evaluation, so the breadth of applicability to genuinely unseen object categories (e.g., very different geometry/texture domains) remains unverified.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important practical problem: removing the need for manually annotated first-frame masks in 6D pose estimation/tracking pipelines, which is a real deployment bottleneck.

The overall system design (SOM for annotation-free segmentation + TOM for failure detection/re-registration) is a sensible integration of existing strong components (DINOv2, CLIP, SAM2, FoundationPose) with some original glue modules (HSFA, tracking-loss classifier).

Reformulating tracking-failure detection as a binary classification problem with a learned similarity network is a reasonable and lightweight idea, and the ablation comparing cosine similarity vs. attention-based matching (Table 4) is informative.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided in the appendix (HSFA depth, language injection, DINO fine-tuning), and implementation/training details are described in some depth, which aids partial reproducibility.
Related work section is reasonably comprehensive and situates the contribution with respect to segmentation and tracking literature.
weaknesses: Central claim of being 'annotation-free' and requiring 'no additional training' is in tension with the actual setup: SOM is extensively trained (80,000 steps on 8 A100 GPUs) on a combined pool of essentially all BOP core datasets (LMO, LM, YCBV, HB, TLESS, TUDL, TYOL, RU-APC) and then evaluated on the test splits of the *same* datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V) in Table 2. This raises serious concerns about information leakage across train/test and undermines the paper's framing as a zero-shot, instance-agnostic, training-free system comparable to CNOS/SAM-6D, which are evaluated in a stricter unseen-object protocol.

The categorization of baselines in Table 2 into 'supervised', 'self-supervised' (STORM only), and 'unsupervised' appears arbitrary and self-serving; many of the listed 'unsupervised' baselines (CNOS, SAM-6D) use comparable CAD-rendering strategies without additional per-dataset training, making the comparison not apples-to-apples given STORM's heavy training regime.

Inconsistent and confusing experimental reporting: the baseline described in the main text for Table 1 ('a DINO-based pipeline... followed by segmentation with SAM2') does not match the baseline actually shown in the table ('FP + CNOS'), with no explanation of the discrepancy. Metric scales are also inconsistent across tables (e.g., Table 2 mAP values of 47–89% vs. Appendix Table 6 AP of 94–95% for ostensibly the same module), without clarification of what differs in evaluation protocol.

Qualitative claims of robustness (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) are illustrated with a single anecdotal example (one mug, one camera rotation) rather than systematic, quantified failure/recovery statistics, making it hard to assess how representative or cherry-picked these examples are.

The tracking-failure dataset used to train/evaluate TOM (Appendix F) is synthetically constructed by pairing BOP crops and applying random shifts/cropping/frame-dropping to simulate occlusion and rapid motion; this is a fairly weak proxy for real occlusion and real high-speed motion, and no evaluation on genuinely challenging real-world sequences (e.g., actual fast motion, real occluders) is provided.

Several core design choices lack ablation or justification: the number of reference views (16), the choice and impact of the specific VLM (gemma-3n) for semantic descriptions, and the sensitivity of the failure-detection threshold are not analyzed, despite these being central to the proposed pipeline.

Reported results lack any variance/error bars or multiple-seed evaluation, and comparisons largely consist of single-run numbers, limiting confidence in the significance of the reported improvements (e.g., the small margins over FP+CNOS in Table 1).

Degree of genuine methodological novelty is modest: much of the system is an assembly of existing pretrained foundation models (DINOv2, CLIP, SAM2, FoundationPose, an LLM/VLM) with added attention-fusion and classification heads; the core technical contributions (HSFA, tracking classifier) are relatively standard attention/MLP constructions.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical bottleneck — removing the need for manually annotated first-frame masks in 6D pose estimation/tracking — which is a meaningful contribution for deployment in robotics/manufacturing settings.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple standard BOP benchmarks (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V) for both segmentation quality and full pose-estimation pipelines, with comparisons against supervised, unsupervised and self-supervised baselines.

The tracking-loss classifier (TOM) is a simple, lightweight and intuitively appealing reformulation of failure detection as a learned classification problem rather than ad hoc thresholding, and the reported overhead (~13 ms) is modest relative to the accuracy gains shown in Table 3.
Reasonably thorough ablations (language injection via AdaNorm-Zero, number of HSFA layers, DINOv2 fine-tuning) that help clarify design choices and their respective costs/benefits.
The paper commits to open-sourcing code and a newly constructed tracking-failure dataset, which, if released as promised, would aid reproducibility and benefit the community.
weaknesses: The claim of an "annotation-free" and "without additional training" system (abstract) is in tension with the actual setup: SOM requires large-scale supervised-style training (80k steps on 8 A100 GPUs using BOP training data with implicit mask/pose supervision from renders), and TOM requires its own dedicated training dataset and procedure. This should be clarified and the terminology ("self-supervised"/"annotation-free") is used loosely and somewhat inconsistently across the Methods/Results/Table 2 categorization, which risks overstating the contribution.

In Table 1, STORM's YCB-Video numbers (0.78/0.99/0.74) are reported as exactly identical to the ground-truth-mask upper bound, which is surprising for an automatically generated segmentation/pose pipeline; no explanation, variance, or statistical analysis is given, raising concern about rounding, cherry-picking, or insufficiently fine-grained evaluation.

The categorization of methods into "self-supervised," "supervised," and "unsupervised" in Table 2 appears to be drawn in a way that conveniently places STORM in its own best-performing category; several "unsupervised" BOP baselines arguably use comparable priors (3D models, rendered views), making the comparison categories questionable and the claimed state-of-the-art position less clear-cut.

The language-injection module depends on an LLM (gemma-3n-E4B-it) and CLIP encoding per object, adding non-trivial latency (0.265s vs 0.196s per Table 5) and potential nondeterminism; this tension with the paper's "real-time" framing is not discussed, and robustness of the LLM-generated descriptions (sensitivity to prompt, hallucination risk) is not analyzed.

TOM is evaluated primarily on a synthetically perturbed version of YCB-Video (random frame dropping, random masking) and a custom in-house dataset constructed by the authors; there is no evaluation on an independent, established occlusion/fast-motion tracking benchmark, limiting confidence in generalization of the failure-detection mechanism.

Reported results lack variance/uncertainty estimates (e.g., over multiple seeds or test splits), and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3, Fig. 4) show single illustrative examples rather than systematic failure-mode analysis.

The overall system is a sophisticated integration of several existing frozen foundation models (DINOv2, SAM2, CLIP, an LLM, FoundationPose) with one new trainable attention module (HSFA) and one small classifier (TOM); the core technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the scope of engineering integration, and the paper would benefit from clearer articulation of what is conceptually new versus combined.

No explicit discussion of limitations, failure cases, or ethical/safety considerations (e.g., behavior when objects are entirely novel/untextured, reliance on 3D CAD models which may not always be available, or risks of repeated LLM calls in deployment) beyond a brief forward-looking "future work" paragraph.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underserved problem: closing the loop between reference-conditioned segmentation, pose tracking, and automatic failure detection/recovery, rather than treating these as independent modules.

Extensive experimental coverage across five BOP benchmarks (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V) for segmentation quality, plus LM-O/YCB-V for full pose tracking, with comparisons against both annotation-free and supervised baselines.

The TOM tracking-loss verifier with an energy-like score and temporal (EMA + L-consecutive-frame) smoothing is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated design; Appendix H.2's ablation showing the temporal policy reduces false re-localization from ~80-89% to ~2-3% is a convincing internal validation of this specific design choice.
Detailed implementation appendices (training hyperparameters, loss weights, augmentation, runtime profiling per component) support reproducibility of the described pipeline architecture.

The limitations section is candid, explicitly clarifying that the 'zero-shot'/annotation-free claim does not imply category-disjoint novel-object generalization, and noting dependence on frozen third-party components (SAM3D, FoundationPose).
weaknesses: Table 2 contains suspicious duplicate values: CosyPose and Mask R-CNN report identical mAP scores to one decimal place on four of five datasets (LM-O: 37.5/37.5, T-LESS: 54.4/54.4, TUD-L: 48.9/48.9, HB: 47.1/47.1), differing only on YCB-V. Since these are architecturally distinct, independently published methods, this pattern is implausible and raises serious concerns about the correctness or provenance of the baseline numbers used for comparison, undermining confidence in the reported state-of-the-art claims.

Many reported baseline numbers throughout the tables (e.g., Table 1's FP+CNOS and FP+GT rows) are suspiciously round (whole numbers to one decimal), inconsistent with typical precision of numbers copied directly from source papers/leaderboards, further raising reproducibility/provenance concerns for the comparison baselines.

The code availability footnote is left blank ('Code available at .'), meaning no actual repository is provided despite claims of reproducibility; this undercuts the otherwise detailed appendix-level documentation.

The central novelty is somewhat incremental: HSFA is largely a composition of standard self-/cross-attention with AdaLN/FiLM conditioning, and the system leans heavily on several frozen foundation models (DINOv3, SAM3D, CLIP/VLM, FoundationPose), so the genuinely new machinery is limited to the fusion architecture and the BCE-trained compatibility verifier.

The 'zero-shot' framing is potentially misleading on first read of the abstract/intro (before the limitations section clarifies it); the training and test splits share object identities, so the strong segmentation numbers do not demonstrate generalization to truly novel object categories, which is the more practically demanding and scientifically interesting setting.

Ablations for TOM's synthetic failure dataset construction (identity-confusion and drift crops generated via random shifts/crops) may not fully capture the diversity of real-world drift patterns; while the YCB-V stress test partially addresses this, the failure/threshold calibration itself is still derived from the same synthetic-data distribution.

Quantitative gains in tracking recovery (Table 4) are demonstrated only against a single baseline (FoundationPose without recovery) rather than against other tracking-loss-aware baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., particle filters, histogram-matching recovery heuristics), limiting the strength of the comparative claim in RQ4/RQ5.

Qualitative results (Fig. 3, Fig. 4) are limited to a small number of illustrative examples, which is insufficient to fully substantiate robustness claims under 'severe occlusions and rapid viewpoint changes' referenced in the abstract.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem: robust, annotation-free 6D pose tracking with automatic failure detection and recovery, which is clearly motivated by real deployment pain points (CAD dependency, manual masking, silent drift).

The TOM module's idea of framing tracking-loss detection as a learned, BCE-trained compatibility verifier with an energy-like score and temporal smoothing is a sensible, well-motivated design, and the appendix ablation on transient noise suppression (Table 9) is a nice sanity check.
Extensive appendix material (algorithm pseudocode, metric definitions, training/augmentation details, runtime profiling) suggests an attempt at thorough documentation.

Quantitative results on BOP benchmarks (Table 2) show the segmentation module (SOM) is competitive with or exceeds several annotation-free and even supervised baselines on multiple datasets, and the single-reference efficient operation (22 FPS) is appealing if verified.
weaknesses: Core novelty is limited: the actual 6D pose estimation/tracking is performed entirely by a frozen, off-the-shelf FoundationPose backend; STORM's only trainable components are a segmentation-fusion module (HSFA) and a binary compatibility classifier (TOM). Describing this as a 'unified framework for 6D pose tracking' overstates the contribution, which is really an improved mask proposer plus a drift detector bolted onto an existing tracker.

The 'zero-shot'/'annotation-free' framing is used prominently throughout the abstract, introduction, and title motivation, but is substantially walked back in Section 4 and the limitations ('the same benchmark object identities may appear in BOP train and test splits, so this should not be read as category-disjoint novel-object generalization'). This caveat should be foregrounded, not buried, since it materially changes how the main claims should be interpreted.

Several headline numbers look suspiciously coarse/round (Table 1: 57.0, 68.0, 41.0, 74.0, 89.0, 53.0, 78.0, 93.0, 56.0, 73.0, 92.0, 69.0, 77.0, 98.0, 73.0) despite claiming 5-seed std; this pattern, combined with the lack of any baseline variance reporting, raises reproducibility and trustworthiness concerns about how these comparisons were actually produced.

Internal inconsistency in reported numbers: Table 8 reports HSFA7 achieving 95.4% AP on 'the test set,' while the main benchmark results in Table 2 report STORM's full mAP as 67.7%. These are never reconciled or clearly distinguished (different protocol/dataset?), making it hard to trust the ablation conclusions.

Comparisons for the core tracking-robustness claim (RQ4, Table 4) are only against vanilla FoundationPose tracking with no failure detection; no comparison against simpler/cheaper failure-detection heuristics (periodic re-initialization, FoundationPose's own uncertainty if any, photometric/IoU consistency checks) is provided, so it is unclear how much of the gain is attributable specifically to the learned TOM verifier versus any re-initialization policy.

The method depends on a large stack of frozen foundation models (SAM3, DINOv3, CLIP/VLM, SAM3D, FoundationPose), several of which are extremely recent (2025) and not yet broadly validated/reproducible in the community; this creates a fragile, hard-to-reproduce pipeline and makes it difficult to isolate STORM's actual contribution from the quality of these underlying black boxes.

Reproducibility is undermined by practical omissions: the code link is blank ('Code available at .'), the Conflict of Interest Disclosure section is empty, and the claimed 'Tracking Failure Benchmark' contribution is not clearly released or described as a public artifact.

SOM training uses additional data beyond standard BOP training splits (SA-V, RUAPC) plus synthetic multi-view renders, which is not matched by the compared annotation-free BOP leaderboard baselines; the 'new SOTA on 4/5 benchmarks' claim may partly reflect this extra data/training budget rather than purely architectural gains (HSFA), and this confound is not controlled for.

The SAM3D geometric anchor is shown (Table 3, Fig. 8) to require a CAD-based similarity-transform alignment step to be usable under BOP evaluation, and the paper admits raw (unaligned) reconstructions perform far worse (VSD 22 vs 61); this undercuts the 'annotation-free from a single image' narrative since benchmark-quality geometry still implicitly leans on CAD-based calibration.

Writing and figure quality show signs of insufficient polish for a submission (an informal transition sentence 'Let us now discuss the literature related to STORM', a stray 'SOM' where 'HSFA' was clearly intended in Section 2.1, garbled appendix figure captions/axis labels), suggesting limited proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: annotation-free, reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking coupled with an explicit mechanism for detecting and recovering from tracking drift, which is a real deployment gap in existing pipelines (e.g., FoundationPose) that silently fail under occlusion/viewpoint change.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple standard BOP benchmarks (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V), comparing against a wide range of annotation-free and supervised baselines, with STORM's segmentation module (SOM) achieving competitive or state-of-the-art mAP while running efficiently (~22 FPS).

The TOM module's design choices are supported by targeted ablations: attention-based compatibility scoring clearly outperforms cosine-similarity baselines (Table 5), and the temporal EMA+persistence decision rule is shown to meaningfully suppress false re-localizations compared to naive per-frame thresholding (Table 9).

Extensive appendix with implementation and training details (loss functions, hyperparameters, data augmentation, dataset construction for the verifier, runtime profiling) supports partial reproducibility of individual components.

The limitations section is candid, explicitly clarifying that the 'zero-shot'/annotation-free claim does not imply category-disjoint novel-object generalization, and acknowledging dependence on frozen backbone quality (SAM3D, FoundationPose) and unresolved cases (transparent/reflective/symmetric objects).
weaknesses: No functional code release is provided (the footnote link is empty), and the pipeline depends on an assembly of several very recent, large frozen foundation models (DINOv3, CLIP/VLM, SAM3D, FoundationPose), making faithful third-party reproduction difficult despite detailed hyperparameter listings.

Table 1 baseline numbers (FP+CNOS, FP+GT) are reported with no decimal precision while STORM's own numbers include two-decimal means and stds, raising questions about whether baselines were re-run under identical conditions or copied from another source with reduced precision; this inconsistency undercuts confidence in the head-to-head comparison central to RQ1.

The core 6D pose registration/tracking backbone (FoundationPose) is used frozen and unmodified; the technical contribution is essentially a stronger mask/reference-conditioning module (HSFA, which combines fairly standard cross-attention, FiLM/AdaLN conditioning, and multi-view aggregation) plus a BCE-trained verifier whose 'energy-like' framing is largely a relabeling of a logit threshold with EMA smoothing — a solid but incremental combination of known components rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The TOM stress-test evaluation relies on synthetic corruptions (independent random frame dropping, random rectangular occlusion masks) rather than naturally occurring hard sequences, which may not fully represent real failure modes such as correlated occlusion or genuine fast motion blur.

Several BOP-leaderboard baselines compared against in Table 2 (NOCTIS, LDSeg, MUSE, NIDS, Prisma-MPG-Complex, ViewInvDet) lack peer-reviewed descriptions and may differ in training data/protocol from STORM, which itself uses an expanded training mix (SA-V, RUAPC) beyond the core BOP sets—this could confound the 'fair comparison' claim.

Minor presentation inconsistencies (e.g., 'This design gives SOM a learned alternative... while keeping HSFA tailored to...' conflating SOM/HSFA terminology, an empty 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure' heading) suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass before camera-ready.
